parts.context: Two coordinators at a home-care agency are dealing with a problem involving one of their clients.

lines: Farid, I need to talk to you about Mr. Kowalski. His daughter called this morning, and she was pretty upset.
Kowalski… the gentleman on Birch Avenue, with Parkinson’s? I thought things were going well there.

They were, until Gloria went on maternity leave. Since then, we’ve sent three different support workers in two weeks, and yesterday he refused to let the new one in. He kept her standing on the porch and told her to go home.
Oh no. So he missed his morning visit completely?

He missed his shower and his medication reminder. And that’s the part that worries me. His Parkinson’s medication has to be taken on a strict schedule. When he’s late, his tremor gets much worse, and he’s already had two falls this year.
Did the daughter say why he refused? Was there a problem with the worker?

Not really. He told his daughter he’s tired of explaining his life to strangers. Every new person asks the same questions and does things in a different order, and he gets flustered. Gloria knew his routine inside out.
That’s fair, honestly. I’d probably feel the same. Is the daughter able to step in for a few days?
She lives in Moncton and works full-time, so no. She’s asking us to guarantee the same worker every day until Gloria comes back.
Every day for a year? We can’t promise that to anyone. Our scheduling just doesn’t work that way.
I know. But we need to offer her something better than what’s happening now, or she’s going to file a complaint with the health authority. And frankly, she’d have a point.

qs.q: Why did Mr. Kowalski refuse to let the new support worker in?
o: She arrived much later than scheduled.
She did not know how to give him his medication properly.
He was frustrated by the constant changes in staff.
His daughter told him not to let her in.
qs.ev: tired of explaining his life to strangers
qs.x: After three workers in two weeks, he is tired of explaining his routine to strangers. Leanne says there was no real problem with the worker herself, and his daughter did not tell him to refuse.

qs.q: Why is Leanne especially concerned about the missed visit?
o: A late dose could make him unsteady.
He had refused several visits before.
The worker reported him to the authority.
His daughter must fly in from Moncton.
qs.ev: When he’s late, his tremor gets much worse, and he’s already had two falls this year.
qs.x: A late dose worsens his tremor, and he has already fallen twice, so the missed reminder raises his fall risk. The complaint to the health authority is something the daughter might make, not the worker.

qs.q: What is Farid’s attitude toward the daughter’s request?
o: He thinks it is reasonable and easy to arrange.
He thinks she should care for her father herself.
He thinks Gloria should return to work early.
He sympathizes with the client but can’t promise it.
qs.ev: Every day for a year? We can’t promise that to anyone.
qs.x: He says the client’s reaction is “fair” but that guaranteeing one worker daily for a year is impossible. He asks whether the daughter can help briefly, not that she take over care.

lines: Okay. What if we assign one of our senior workers, say Rosa, to his mornings? She’s great with Parkinson’s clients.

I thought about Rosa. But she already has six regular clients, and her last morning visit is in the north end. Birch Avenue is forty minutes from there. She’d be late every single day, and with his medication timing, late is the one thing we can’t be.
Right. What about moving his visit to the afternoon? Then Rosa could fit him in after her north-end clients.
His medication is at eight. That’s why the visit is in the morning. Unless his doctor changes the schedule, an afternoon visit doesn’t solve anything.
Fair. Okay, here’s another thought. Instead of one worker, we pick two, and only two. They alternate, and nobody else goes in. He’d get to know both of them.
That’s better than three strangers in two weeks. But he’d still have to explain everything twice.

Not if we write it all down properly. Gloria could record a detailed care routine: the order he likes things done, how he takes his pills, even which radio station he likes on in the morning. She’s on leave, but she messaged the team chat last week, so she’s clearly still in touch.
Hmm. I’d be careful asking someone on maternity leave to do work for us. Technically, we’re not supposed to contact staff on leave about work at all.
Then not work, exactly. Just a phone call with the new workers, if she offers. I bet she’d want to.
Maybe. Let me check with HR before anyone contacts her.

qs.q: Why can’t Rosa take over Mr. Kowalski’s mornings?
o: She has no experience with Parkinson’s clients.
She would not be able to arrive on time.
She already visits him in the afternoons.
She is about to go on leave herself.
qs.ev: She’d be late every single day
qs.x: Her previous client is forty minutes away, so she would always be late, which his medication schedule cannot allow. Farid actually says she is great with Parkinson’s clients.

qs.q: Why does Leanne reject moving the visit to the afternoon?
o: Rosa’s afternoons are already fully booked.
His daughter prefers that he be seen early.
The visit is tied to when he takes his pills.
His doctor has refused to change his schedule.
qs.ev: His medication is at eight. That’s why the visit is in the morning.
qs.x: The morning visit exists because his medication is due at eight. The doctor has not refused anything – Leanne only says the schedule would have to be changed by the doctor.

qs.q: How does Leanne feel about asking Gloria for help?
o: Uneasy, because it may break workplace rules
Confident, because Gloria offered last week
Opposed, because Gloria is moving away
Enthusiastic, as long as Gloria is paid
qs.ev: I’d be careful asking someone on maternity leave to do work for us.
qs.x: She hesitates because staff on leave should not be contacted about work, and wants to check with HR. Gloria messaged the team chat but did not offer to help.

lines: Okay, I talked to HR. We can’t ask Gloria to do anything, but if she contacts us herself, she can share whatever she likes. And as it turns out, she already has. She heard about Mr. Kowalski through the grapevine and emailed me a two-page routine for him this morning.
Of course she did. That’s Gloria. So, two workers alternating, and they both follow her routine?

Yes, and I’d like it to be Rosa and Daniel. Rosa can’t do weekday mornings, but she can do weekends, because her weekend schedule is much lighter. Daniel lives five minutes from Birch Avenue and has weekday mornings open.
So Daniel Monday to Friday and Rosa on weekends. And nobody else, even if someone calls in sick?
If Daniel’s sick, Rosa covers, even if it means she’s a bit late, and we call Mr. Kowalski to warn him. I’d rather he got a familiar face late than a stranger on time.
Hmm, I’m not sure his daughter would agree with you on that, given the medication.
That’s why I want to set up a pill dispenser with an alarm. Then the medication reminder doesn’t depend on anyone walking through the door. The pharmacy can have one ready by Thursday.
Good idea. Do you want me to call the daughter?

No, I should. She’s already spoken to me, and she deserves to hear it from the same person. But could you introduce Daniel to Mr. Kowalski tomorrow? Bring him along on the first visit, so it’s not another stranger at the door.
Sure. I’ll meet Daniel at the house at eight.

qs.q: What is Leanne’s plan if Daniel is sick?
o: A new worker will be sent on time.
The daughter will be asked to visit.
Farid will cover the visit himself.
Rosa will go, even if she arrives late.
qs.ev: If Daniel’s sick, Rosa covers, even if it means she’s a bit late
qs.x: Rosa covers even if she is late, because Leanne prefers a familiar face to a stranger. Sending a new worker on time is exactly what she wants to avoid.

qs.q: What will Farid do tomorrow?
o: Call Mr. Kowalski’s daughter with the plan
Go with the new worker on his first visit
Pick up a pill dispenser from the pharmacy
Ask HR whether Gloria may be contacted
qs.ev: Bring him along on the first visit
qs.x: Leanne asks Farid to introduce Daniel by attending the first visit, and he agrees to meet him at eight. Leanne will call the daughter herself, and the dispenser is ready Thursday.

parts.context: A man is speaking with an optician after his eye exam.

lines: Okay, Darnell, the optometrist has sent over your new prescription. Your distance vision has changed a fair bit since your last exam, which explains the headaches you mentioned when you’re driving at night.
That’s a relief, actually. I was worried it was something more serious. So I need new glasses?
You do. Now, your work benefits cover glasses up to three hundred dollars every two years. According to our system, your last claim was twenty-six months ago, so you’re eligible again.
Great. I really like the frames I have now. Could you just put new lenses in them?

We can, but I wouldn’t recommend it with these. The hinge on the left side is cracked – see here? If it breaks while we’re fitting the lenses, we’re not responsible, and you’d end up paying for new frames anyway.
Oh. I hadn’t noticed that. Okay, new frames, then. What about those thin lenses I’ve seen advertised?

High-index lenses. With your prescription, they’d make a real difference – about a third thinner. They’re an extra hundred and twenty dollars. And since you drive a lot at night, I’d suggest the anti-glare coating, which is another sixty.
So if I pick a frame for, say, two hundred, that’s… well over three hundred.
It is, but we have a promotion this month. If you buy a complete pair, a second pair of prescription sunglasses is half price.
Hmm. I’m not really a sunglasses person. I’d rather keep the cost down. Can I skip the thin lenses?
Honestly, with your prescription, standard lenses would be quite thick at the edges, especially in a larger frame. If you go with a smaller frame, though, the difference is much less noticeable.
Okay, then let’s look at the smaller frames, and keep the anti-glare. Night driving is the whole reason I’m here.
That makes sense. The smaller frames start at a hundred and forty. Glasses take about ten business days, and we’ll text you when they’re ready.
Ten days. And I can keep wearing my old ones until then?
Yes, but avoid driving at night if you can. Your old prescription is quite a bit off now.

qs.q: Why is Darnell relieved?
o: His benefits will cover the full cost.
His headaches have a simple explanation.
His old frames can be used again.
His prescription has not changed.
qs.ev: which explains the headaches you mentioned when you’re driving at night
qs.x: His changed prescription explains the headaches, and he had feared something more serious. His prescription has changed “a fair bit”, so the last option is wrong.

qs.q: Why does Siobhan advise against reusing his current frames?
o: They are too small for high-index lenses.
They are more than two years old.
They are not covered by his benefits.
They are damaged and could break.
qs.ev: The hinge on the left side is cracked
qs.x: The cracked hinge could break during fitting, and the shop would not be responsible. Twenty-six months refers to his last claim, not the frames’ age as a reason.

qs.q: What is Darnell’s reaction to the sunglasses promotion?
o: He isn’t interested because it adds cost.
He plans to buy a second pair later.
He wants to use the offer for night driving.
He thinks it is too good to be true.
qs.ev: I’m not really a sunglasses person. I’d rather keep the cost down.
qs.x: He politely declines because he doesn’t wear sunglasses and wants to save money. Night driving is his reason for choosing the anti-glare coating, not sunglasses.

qs.q: What does Siobhan suggest as a way to manage without high-index lenses?
o: Choosing standard lenses with anti-glare
Waiting for next month’s promotion
Selecting a more compact frame
Buying prescription sunglasses instead
qs.ev: If you go with a smaller frame, though, the difference is much less noticeable.
qs.x: A smaller frame reduces how thick standard lenses look at the edges. Anti-glare is a separate feature that does not affect thickness.

qs.q: What does Siobhan advise him to do until his new glasses arrive?
o: Stop wearing his old glasses completely
Limit his driving after dark
Come back for a second eye exam
Use his old frames with temporary lenses
qs.ev: avoid driving at night if you can
qs.x: She says he can wear his old glasses but should avoid night driving because the prescription is out of date. She does not tell him to stop wearing them.

parts.context: A woman is calling a public health office about prenatal classes.

lines: Riverbend Public Health, prenatal services. This is Joon speaking.
Hi, Joon. My name is Valentina. I’m about twenty-two weeks pregnant with my first, and my doctor suggested I sign up for prenatal classes. I was hoping you could tell me what’s available.

Congratulations! Sure. We have three options. The most popular is our six-week evening series. It runs on Tuesdays from six-thirty to eight-thirty here at the Riverbend office, starting January twelfth. It’s forty dollars per couple, and that includes a support person – a partner, a friend, a family member, whoever you like.
Tuesdays. Hmm. My partner, Mateo, works evening shifts at the hospital, and Tuesday is always one of his nights.

Then you might prefer the weekend intensive. It covers the same material over two Saturdays, from nine to three. The next one is February sixth and thirteenth. It’s sixty dollars per couple, and lunch is included.
That could work. Would that be too early, though? I’m due at the beginning of April.

Not at all. We usually recommend starting between twenty-four and twenty-eight weeks, so you’d be right in that window. If people take classes too early, they tend to forget a lot by the time the baby arrives.
Makes sense. And what’s the third option?

An online, self-paced course. It’s free, it has eight modules, and you have access for six months. Some people use it on its own, but honestly, I find it works best as a review alongside one of the in-person options. Online, you miss the chance to ask questions and to practise things like breathing and positions with your partner.
Right. I think in-person would be better for us. Is the sixty dollars a problem if money’s tight? We’re on one income at the moment.
We can waive the fee for families who need it. You’d just tick the box on the registration form. Nobody asks for proof.
Oh, that’s kind. And do we need to bring anything?
Two pillows and a yoga mat or a thick blanket. We do a fair bit of practice on the floor. Parking is free on Saturdays.
Great. My doctor also mentioned a hospital tour.

That’s booked directly through the hospital, not through us, and they only take people who are at least thirty weeks along. There’s also a separate free breastfeeding class on Thursday afternoons, which we suggest after thirty-two weeks.
Thursday afternoons are fine; I’m off work then. Okay, so how do I register for the weekend one?
Online, on our website. Registration closes one week before the first class, but the weekend sessions fill quickly, so I wouldn’t wait.

qs.q: Why might the Tuesday series not suit Valentina?
o: It starts too early in her pregnancy.
It doesn’t allow a support person.
Her partner usually works that evening.
It costs more than the weekend class.
qs.ev: Tuesday is always one of his nights
qs.x: Mateo works evening shifts, always including Tuesdays, so he could not attend. The Tuesday series actually costs less ($40) than the weekend one ($60).

qs.q: What does Joon say about the timing of the weekend course?
o: It falls in the recommended stage of pregnancy.
It is too early for someone due in April.
It is the only course available before April.
It is best taken after thirty-two weeks.
qs.ev: so you’d be right in that window
qs.x: February falls within the recommended 24–28 week window for her. Thirty-two weeks is the suggested time for the breastfeeding class, not prenatal classes.

qs.q: What is Joon’s opinion of the online course?
o: It is better value than the in-person classes.
It should be used only by people who work evenings.
It covers more material than the weekend course.
It is most useful as an extra to a live class.
qs.ev: I find it works best as a review alongside one of the in-person options
qs.x: He says it works best as a review alongside in-person classes, because online you cannot ask questions or practise. He never compares its value or content to the other courses.

qs.q: What must Valentina do to have the fee waived?
o: Provide proof of her household income
Indicate her need on the sign-up form
Ask her doctor to write a letter
Attend the Tuesday series instead
qs.ev: You’d just tick the box on the registration form.
qs.x: She simply ticks a box when registering; Joon stresses that nobody asks for proof, so the first option is wrong.

qs.q: What does Joon say about the hospital tour?
o: It is included in the weekend course.
It is held on Thursday afternoons.
It is arranged separately, later in pregnancy.
It is booked through the public health office.
qs.ev: That’s booked directly through the hospital, not through us, and they only take people who are at least thirty weeks along.
qs.x: The hospital books the tour itself and requires at least thirty weeks. Thursday afternoons are for the breastfeeding class, not the tour.

qs.q: What does Joon suggest Valentina do?
o: Register soon, because spaces are limited
Wait until a week before the first class
Call again once she reaches thirty weeks
Sign up for the online course first
qs.ev: the weekend sessions fill quickly, so I wouldn’t wait
qs.x: Registration is open until a week before, but because weekend sessions fill quickly, he advises registering now. Waiting until the deadline is the risk he warns against.

parts.context: You will hear a news report about a new emergency response program.

lines: Starting next month, residents of Marlow County who are trained in CPR will be able to sign up for a smartphone app that alerts them when someone nearby goes into cardiac arrest. The program, called HeartNear, will notify registered volunteers within five hundred metres of a 911 call for a suspected cardiac arrest in a public place, and direct them to the closest automated external defibrillator, or AED. The county is also adding one hundred and twenty AEDs to public buildings, arenas and transit stations, bringing the total to just over three hundred. Each one will be registered in the app. Volunteers must be at least eighteen and hold a current CPR certificate. They are not expected to enter private homes; alerts will only be sent for incidents in public spaces. Deputy Chief Rekha Pillai of the county’s paramedic service says the first few minutes are critical.

For every minute without CPR, a person’s chance of survival drops by roughly ten percent. Our paramedics are fast, but in rural parts of the county, it can take twelve or fifteen minutes to reach a patient. A bystander who starts compressions and gets an AED on someone in the first four or five minutes can genuinely double their chances. We’re not asking people to be heroes. We’re asking them to push hard and fast until we get there.

Similar programs in other regions have recruited thousands of volunteers, though officials admit that most alerts are not accepted, often because volunteers are busy or too far away. The county says it expects about one alert in four to be answered. Some residents have raised concerns about being held legally responsible if something goes wrong. The province’s Good Samaritan law protects people who help in an emergency in good faith, and the county says volunteers will receive a short online briefing on what to expect, including how to cope with the stress afterwards. Free CPR courses will be offered at county libraries through the winter for anyone who wants to get certified before signing up.

qs.q: When will volunteers receive an alert?
o: Whenever anyone calls 911 in their area
During a nearby public cardiac emergency
When an AED is used in their neighbourhood
When paramedics are too far away to help
qs.ev: within five hundred metres of a 911 call for a suspected cardiac arrest in a public place
qs.x: Alerts go out only for suspected cardiac arrests in public places within 500 metres. Not every 911 call triggers one, and private homes are excluded.

qs.q: What does Deputy Chief Pillai mainly want to emphasize?
o: Paramedics in rural areas need more funding.
Volunteers should avoid entering private homes.
AEDs should be installed in every building.
Early help from bystanders saves lives.
qs.ev: can genuinely double their chances
qs.x: She stresses that CPR and an AED in the first minutes can double survival. Rural delays are her reason why bystanders matter, not a call for funding.

qs.q: What does Pillai mean when she says “We’re not asking people to be heroes”?
o: Volunteers need only keep doing CPR until help comes.
Most volunteers will rarely be asked to respond at all.
Volunteers should never attempt CPR on their own.
Volunteers will be paid a small fee for each call.
qs.ev: We’re asking them to push hard and fast until we get there.
qs.x: She means volunteers just need to do chest compressions until paramedics arrive – nothing more dramatic. How often they will be alerted is a separate point made later.

qs.q: What do officials expect about the alerts?
o: Most will be accepted within five minutes.
Thousands will be sent in the first month.
Only a minority of them will be answered.
Most will be sent to rural volunteers.
qs.ev: The county says it expects about one alert in four to be answered.
qs.x: One in four means most alerts will go unanswered. “Thousands” refers to volunteers recruited in other regions, not alerts.

qs.q: How is the county responding to concerns about legal responsibility?
o: It will provide lawyers for volunteers.
It notes helpers are protected by an existing law.
It will make every volunteer sign a legal waiver.
It will only send alerts to paramedics.
qs.ev: The province’s Good Samaritan law protects people who help in an emergency in good faith
qs.x: The report points to the existing Good Samaritan law that protects helpers acting in good faith. No waiver or lawyers are mentioned; volunteers get an online briefing.

parts.context: Three members of an elementary school’s parent council are discussing a new school lunch program.

lines: Okay, everyone, the main item tonight is the lunch program. The province has confirmed our grant: three dollars and fifty cents per student per day. Anything above that, families cover, with a pay-what-you-can option. We have two vendor proposals, and we need to recommend one to the principal by Friday.

Right. So FreshPlate Catering is six twenty-five a meal, which means families would pay two seventy-five a day on top of the grant. Harvest Table, the co-op, is five ten, so families would pay a dollar sixty. Over a full school year, that difference adds up to more than two hundred dollars per child.

Money matters, but for me the first question is allergies. We have eleven kids at this school with severe nut allergies, including my son. FreshPlate’s kitchen is certified nut-free. Harvest Table’s isn’t.
I asked Harvest Table about that. They said they could prepare our meals on a dedicated day each week, when no nuts are used in the kitchen at all, and freeze them.
Frozen meals reheated in a school microwave? That’s not exactly the fresh, local food they’re advertising. And ‘no nuts that day’ is not the same as certified.

Fair point. I’ll also admit I was keen on Harvest Table mainly because of the price, but when I looked closer, there’s another problem. They can only deliver four days a week. They have one van, and they serve two other schools.
Exactly. Families would pack lunch on Fridays, which kind of defeats the purpose of a universal program.
Does it, though? The research the province sent us says the biggest benefit is for kids who come to school without enough food. Four good meals a week is a lot better than zero.
I don’t disagree with that. But let’s be honest about the food, too. I looked at both menus. FreshPlate’s is basically chicken fingers, pasta and pizza, with a side of carrots nobody will touch.
Which is exactly what kids will actually eat. There’s no point serving lentil curry if half of it ends up in the garbage.
Harvest Table said they’d run tasting days first, so the kids can vote on recipes. And their meals have about twice as many vegetables.
Okay, I’ll be honest. I came in tonight ready to vote for FreshPlate because of the allergy issue. But if Harvest Table can actually get certified, I could live with it.
They told me they’ve applied for certification. Their inspection is next month.

Then why not make that a condition? We recommend Harvest Table for one term, as a pilot, on the condition that their certification is approved before the first delivery. If it isn’t, we go with FreshPlate.
And nothing frozen on a so-called nut-free day in the meantime. I want that in writing.
Families pack lunch on Fridays, and the council could use some of our fundraising money for healthy snacks for kids who need them. It’s not perfect, but it’s a start.
I like that. We’ll also survey the kids after six weeks to see what they’re actually eating.
Fine. One term, conditional on certification, and a survey at six weeks. I’ll write up the allergy requirements for the contract.
Great. I’ll draft the recommendation for the principal tomorrow.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of the meeting?
o: To apply for a provincial lunch grant
To set the price that families will pay
To choose recipes for the tasting days
To decide which supplier to recommend
qs.ev: we need to recommend one to the principal by Friday
qs.x: They must recommend one of two vendors to the principal. The grant is already confirmed, and tasting days are a vendor’s offer, not the meeting’s goal.

qs.q: According to Doug’s figures, how much more per day would families pay with FreshPlate than with Harvest Table?
o: Two dollars and seventy-five cents
One dollar and fifteen cents
One dollar and sixty cents
Six dollars and twenty-five cents
qs.ev: Harvest Table, the co-op, is five ten, so families would pay a dollar sixty.
qs.x: Families would pay $2.75 with FreshPlate and $1.60 with Harvest Table, a difference of $1.15. $2.75 is FreshPlate’s family share, not the difference.

qs.q: Why does Ngozi doubt Harvest Table’s offer of a dedicated nut-free day?
o: It is not the same as official certification.
Her son does not like frozen meals.
The school has no microwave to reheat them.
It would raise the price of each meal.
qs.ev: ‘no nuts that day’ is not the same as certified
qs.x: She says a nut-free day is not equivalent to a certified nut-free kitchen. Her microwave comment criticizes freshness, not the lack of a microwave.

qs.q: How has Doug’s view of Harvest Table changed?
o: He now thinks its menu is too unusual for kids.
He now thinks its price is too high.
He now doubts it can deliver often enough.
He now prefers it for its vegetables.
qs.ev: They can only deliver four days a week.
qs.x: He liked it for the price but now worries it can deliver only four days a week. He never says the price is too high – it is the cheaper option.

qs.q: What is Celeste’s view about having meals only four days a week?
o: It would still help the children most in need.
It defeats the purpose of a universal program.
It would be too expensive for the council.
It should be extended to five days next year.
qs.ev: Four good meals a week is a lot better than zero.
qs.x: She argues that four meals still greatly helps children who lack food. “Defeats the purpose” is Doug’s view, which she challenges.

qs.q: What does Doug suggest about FreshPlate’s menu?
o: It contains too few vegetables.
It is unsafe for children with allergies.
It is too expensive for what it offers.
Children are more likely to finish it.
qs.ev: Which is exactly what kids will actually eat.
qs.x: Doug defends the simple menu because children will eat it rather than waste it. The lack of vegetables is Ngozi’s criticism, not his.

qs.q: What does Ngozi admit about her position?
o: She never had concerns about allergies.
She has softened her earlier position.
She will vote against the pilot.
She prefers the tasting-day plan.
qs.ev: I came in tonight ready to vote for FreshPlate because of the allergy issue.
qs.x: She arrived supporting FreshPlate but says she “could live with” Harvest Table if it is certified. She still cares about allergies and in the end supports the pilot.

qs.q: What will happen if Harvest Table is not certified in time?
o: Meals will be prepared on a nut-free day.
The pilot will be delayed by one term.
The council will use the other vendor.
Families will pack lunch every day.
qs.ev: If it isn’t, we go with FreshPlate.
qs.x: Certification is a condition; without it, they switch to FreshPlate. Ngozi specifically rejects the frozen nut-free-day option.

parts.context: You will hear a radio report about medical notes for short absences from work.

lines: It’s a scene family doctors know well: a patient with a cold or a stomach bug, who is already starting to feel better, sitting in a crowded waiting room for one reason only – their employer wants a note. Doctors’ groups have been arguing for years that these notes are a waste of everyone’s time. One provincial medical association estimates that family physicians write several hundred thousand sick notes a year, many for illnesses lasting two days or less. Doctors point out that they usually have no way to confirm whether someone was actually sick. They simply write down what the patient tells them. Some also raise a public health concern: sending contagious people into clinics, where they sit next to babies and elderly patients, is exactly the opposite of what we want. Several provinces have now passed laws banning employers from requiring a medical note for short absences, typically three days or fewer. But not everyone is pleased. Bruno Castellano owns three bakeries and employs about forty people.

Look, I trust most of my staff. But in a bakery, if two people don’t show up on a Saturday morning, I can’t open on time. Before the new rule, the note was a small deterrent. Since it came in, I’ve noticed more sick days on Mondays and Fridays. I can’t prove anything, and maybe it’s a coincidence. But it’s a pattern.

Labour researchers say the evidence on that point is mixed. Some studies from places with similar rules found no significant increase in absences, while others found a small rise in one-day absences that was offset by fewer long ones, possibly because people stay home early instead of working while sick and getting worse. Employers’ associations have suggested a compromise: allow employers to ask for a note, but let pharmacists or nurses provide it, or accept a simple signed statement from the employee. Doctors’ groups generally support the signed-statement idea, but are less enthusiastic about shifting the paperwork to pharmacists, who they say are already overloaded. Mr. Castellano says he could accept a signed statement.
Honestly, it’s not about the piece of paper. It’s about people taking it seriously. If someone has to sign their name to something that says they were sick, most people won’t lie.

Worker advocates, meanwhile, say the real issue is that many low-wage employees have no paid sick days at all, so they come to work sick anyway, note or no note. They argue that until that changes, the debate over sick notes is missing the point.

qs.q: According to the report, why do doctors object to writing sick notes?
o: They are not paid for writing them.
They cannot actually verify the illness.
Patients often ask for longer absences.
Employers often reject doctors’ notes.
qs.ev: They simply write down what the patient tells them.

p1.meta: From: Odette Brassard | To: Whitney Ng | Subject: Greetings from Cedar Falls (and a small request)
p1.text:
Dear Whitney,

I can hardly believe it has been a year since I left the office and moved out here. You were right that I’d miss the city less than I expected – although I do still dream about that dumpling place near our old office. Cedar Falls has been good to me. It’s small, everyone knows everyone, and I can see the mountains from my kitchen window, which never gets old.

You’ll laugh, but I’ve become a fitness leader of sorts. Last spring I started walking every morning to get to know the town, and a few of my neighbours asked if they could join me. Then their friends joined. Now there are about twenty-five of us, almost all over seventy, who meet at the library at nine every weekday. The town’s public health nurse even comes along once a month to check blood pressure, and a couple of our members tell me their doctors have reduced their medication. I can’t take credit for that, but I’ll admit I’m proud.

The trouble is winter. Last year we walked laps in the arena lobby when the sidewalks iced over, but the arena is being renovated this winter, so that’s no longer an option. The school gym is free in the mornings, and the principal has kindly said yes, but only from nine-thirty to ten-thirty, which is fine. The real problem is getting there. The sidewalks out here aren’t cleared nearly as quickly as in the city, and two of our members fell last January. One broke her wrist and hasn’t been back since. I think she’s lost her confidence more than anything.

Which brings me to my request. You mentioned once that your community centre collects donated ice cleats and walking poles for its seniors’ program. Do you think they would have any spares to share? Even ten pairs of cleats would make a huge difference. Since you’re coming up to visit in January anyway, maybe you could bring them in your car? I’m happy to pay for anything, of course.

I can’t wait to see you. The guest room is ready, and I’ve already planned a walk for us – with cleats!

Warmly,
Odette

p3.title: Growing Better: Gardens Move into Hospitals
paras: On the fourth floor of Bellmont Rehabilitation Hospital, between the physiotherapy gym and the elevators, there is a room that smells of soil. Long tables hold trays of seedlings, herbs and tomato plants, and on a Wednesday afternoon, half a dozen patients are repotting geraniums. Some are recovering from strokes, others from amputations or spinal injuries. This is horticultural therapy, and its supporters say it does far more than pass the time. Gripping a trowel strengthens weakened hands, reaching for a watering can tests balance, and following a planting sequence exercises memory and attention. “Patients will do a hundred repetitions of a movement here that they’d refuse to do ten times in the gym,” says therapist Janelle Okoro. “They’re not exercising. They’re growing something.”

The idea is not new. Hospitals in the nineteenth century often had gardens where patients worked, and veterans returning from the world wars were offered gardening as part of their rehabilitation, often on hospital grounds that were later paved over for parking. What is new is the effort to measure results. Small studies have reported improvements in mood, hand strength and sleep among patients who take part in gardening programs, and some long-term care homes report that residents with dementia are calmer on days when they spend time in a garden. However, researchers acknowledge that many of these studies are too small or too short to support firm conclusions, and that it is difficult to separate the effect of the plants from the attention patients receive from staff.

Cost has kept many programs small. Bellmont’s garden room was built with a donation from a former patient’s family, and the hospital pays for one part-time therapist and a supply budget of about four thousand dollars a year. Volunteers from a local gardening club help with watering and maintenance, and in summer the program moves outside to raised beds that can be reached from a wheelchair. Okoro says the biggest obstacle is not money but space. “Every square metre in a hospital is fought over,” she says. “A garden looks like a luxury until you see what it does.” Infection control teams also had to approve the program, since soil can carry bacteria; patients with weakened immune systems wear gloves and work only with sterilized potting mix.

For patients, the benefits are often personal. Arthur Nakamura, a retired bus driver who lost the use of his left hand after a stroke, says the garden gave him something to look forward to during a three-month stay. “In the gym, they count your repetitions. Here, you watch something get bigger because of you.” Before he was discharged, Arthur planted a row of beans that he will never harvest; the next group of patients will. He says that is part of the point. Okoro agrees. She now runs a short course for staff from other hospitals who want to start their own programs, and she says interest has tripled since last year. Her advice is to start small: “A windowsill and a few pots is enough to begin.”

qs.x: Paragraph C: patients with weak immune systems wear gloves and use sterilized potting mix.

p4.title: Sick People Shouldn’t Have to Pay to Park
p4.byline: Opinion | by Marguerite Lam, patient advocate
p4.text:
Last month, a reader sent me a receipt. It was from the parking garage at a large hospital, and the total was $186. It covered nine days – the time her husband spent in intensive care after a heart attack. She drove in every morning and left every night, because she wanted to be there when the doctors did their rounds. “I would have paid anything to be with him,” she wrote. “But I shouldn’t have had to.”

She is right. Hospital parking fees are one of the quietest and most unfair costs in our health system. We pride ourselves on care that is free at the point of service, yet families visiting dying parents, cancer patients coming for daily radiation, and parents of babies in neonatal units routinely spend hundreds of dollars simply to park. For a low-income family, that can mean choosing between visiting a sick relative and buying groceries.

Hospitals defend the fees on two grounds. The first is money. Parking revenue at large hospitals can reach several million dollars a year, and administrators say it pays for equipment and services that government funding does not cover. I do not doubt it. But that is precisely the problem. We have quietly allowed the sickest people and their families to subsidize the health system, a burden that ought to be shared by all taxpayers. If hospitals need more money, the province should provide it openly, not collect it at a parking gate.

The second argument is that free parking would be abused – that commuters and shoppers would fill the spaces, leaving none for patients. This is a real concern, especially for downtown hospitals. But it is a problem with practical solutions. Several hospitals elsewhere validate parking for patients and registered visitors at the front desk, so that only people with real hospital business park for free. Others offer free parking for the first two hours, which covers most appointments, and charge only after that.

To be fair, some hospitals have made progress. Many now offer discounted weekly or monthly passes for frequent visitors, and a few waive fees for families of palliative patients. These are welcome steps, but they put the burden on exhausted families to know about the discounts, ask for them and often fill out forms. When your child is in surgery, you are not thinking about whether you qualify for a reduced rate. In my experience, most people who would be eligible never hear about these programs.

Critics will say that removing parking fees benefits people who drive, while doing nothing for those who take the bus. That is a fair point, and I would support using some of the money to improve transit to hospitals as well. But we should not let the perfect be the enemy of the good.

The province should require all hospitals to phase out parking fees for patients and their designated visitors within three years, and compensate hospitals for the lost revenue. In the meantime, every hospital should post its discount programs at every entrance and pay station, in plain language. It is a small change that would spare families a great deal of stress at the worst moments of their lives.

t1.situation: Your downstairs neighbour has recently started smoking on their balcony every evening, and the smoke comes into your apartment through your windows. Your young child has asthma. Write an email to your building manager.
bullets: Explain how it is affecting your family
Suggest what the building manager could do
t1.model:
Dear Mr. Haddadi,

I am writing about a problem that has been affecting my family in unit 504 since early September.

The resident directly below us has begun smoking on their balcony several times each evening, usually between seven and eleven o’clock. Because our bedroom windows are right above, the smoke drifts straight into our apartment. Even with the windows closed, we can smell it in the hallway and in our daughter’s room.

For us, this is more than an annoyance. Our four-year-old has asthma, and over the past month she has needed her rescue inhaler almost every night. Her paediatrician has advised us to keep her away from second-hand smoke entirely, which is impossible at the moment. We also have to keep our windows shut on warm evenings, which makes the apartment stuffy.

I would prefer not to create conflict with our neighbour, so I would be grateful if you could remind all residents of the building’s policy, which I understand prohibits smoking on balconies. If that is not effective, perhaps a designated smoking area away from the building could be offered.

Thank you for your help.

Sincerely,
Mina Rostami

t2.intro: Your local community health centre has received funding to hire one new full-time staff member and is asking residents which position it should create.
t2.question: Which option do you prefer? Explain the reasons for your choice.
t2.a: Option A: A registered dietitian who would offer free one-on-one nutrition consultations and weekly group cooking workshops for families.
t2.b: Option B: A mental-health counsellor who would offer free short-term counselling (up to six sessions) for adults and teenagers, with no referral needed.
t2.model:
I would choose Option B, the mental-health counsellor, because it would fill a gap that is currently much harder for residents to fill on their own.

A dietitian would certainly be valuable, and I can see how cooking workshops could help families eat better on a tight budget. However, a great deal of reliable nutrition information is already available for free through public health websites, libraries and community kitchens. Mental-health support is a different story. Private counselling in our area costs well over a hundred dollars a session, and the public waiting lists are months long. For many people, especially teenagers and low-income adults, that means getting no help at all.

The fact that no referral would be needed is also important. Many people never take the first step because they would have to explain their problems to a family doctor first, and some residents do not have one. Six free sessions could help someone through a crisis, such as a job loss or a divorce, before it becomes far more serious.

In the long run, good mental health also makes it easier for people to look after their physical health, including what they eat.

t1.prompt: Your friend has been vaping every day for two years and wants to quit, but has already tried twice and failed. Give your friend some advice about how to quit successfully.
t1.model: First of all, I think it’s great that you want to try again, and honestly, failing twice doesn’t mean you can’t do it. Most people need a few attempts, and each time you learn something. So let’s think about what went wrong before. I’d start by choosing a quit date, maybe two weeks from now, so you have time to prepare. Tell a few people, including me, so we can check in on you. Second, figure out your triggers. You always vape when you’re stressed at work or when you’re out with friends, right? So plan something else for those moments. Chewing gum, a quick walk or even just texting me might help you get through the cravings, which usually only last a few minutes. Third, talk to a pharmacist or your doctor about nicotine patches or lozenges. Quitting nicotine completely and suddenly is really hard, and those products can reduce the withdrawal symptoms. Also, get rid of every vape and pod in your apartment and car. If they’re around, it’s way too easy to give in. Finally, if you slip once, don’t give up completely. One bad day doesn’t erase all your progress. Just start again the next morning.

t2.prompt: Talk about a time when you or someone you know suddenly needed medical help. What happened, and how was the situation handled?
t2.model: A couple of summers ago, I was at a barbecue at my cousin’s house when her father-in-law suddenly started having trouble breathing. At first we thought he was choking, but he said his chest felt tight and his left arm was tingling. My cousin, who’s a nurse, recognized right away that it could be a heart attack. She told me to call 911 while she got him to sit down and loosened his shirt. The dispatcher asked whether he could chew an aspirin, and luckily someone had some in their bag. The paramedics arrived in about ten minutes, which felt like an hour, and took him straight to the hospital. It turned out he had a blocked artery, and he had surgery the next day. He’s completely fine now. What I learned is that staying calm and calling for help immediately really matters.

scene.alt: A snowy park on a cold, sunny winter morning. On the left, a sign on a post reads “WALKING CLUB 9 AM” next to a tall pine tree. Three older adults wearing warm hats are walking in a line along the path: a man in a red jacket at the front holding a map, a woman in a blue coat with long white hair, and a man in a green jacket with glasses. In the middle, a park worker in a grey jacket and orange hat is clearing the path with a shovel. A black dog walks beside the group. On the right, a child in a purple jacket and blue hat is waving both arms next to a snowman. There is a wooden bench covered in snow and another pine tree in the background.

t3.prompt: Describe some things that are happening in the picture as well as you can. The person you are speaking to cannot see the picture.
t3.model: This picture shows a snowy park on a cold but sunny winter morning. On the left, next to a tall pine tree, there’s a sign that says “Walking Club 9 a.m.”, and I think the club has just started its walk. Three older people in warm hats are walking in a line along the path. The man in front is wearing a red jacket and holding a map, so he might be the leader. Behind him, there’s a woman with long white hair in a blue coat and a man in a green jacket with glasses. A black dog is trotting along beside them. In the middle, a park worker in an orange hat is shovelling snow off the path near a snow-covered bench. On the right, a little kid in a purple jacket is waving both arms beside a snowman.

t4.prompt: In this picture, what do you think will most probably happen next?
t4.model: I think the walking group is going to continue along the path, but they’ll probably have to slow down when they reach the part that hasn’t been shovelled yet. The park worker might stop and wave them around the deeper snow, or the leader with the map could decide to take a different route. I can imagine the black dog running ahead and jumping into the snowbank, and someone in the group laughing and calling it back. Meanwhile, the child by the snowman is waving, so maybe the walkers are her grandparents. She’ll probably run over to show them the snowman she built, and they’ll stop to take a picture of it. After that, I think the group will finish their loop and head somewhere warm for a hot drink, because it looks freezing out there.

t5.intro: Your company wants to start a lunchtime wellness activity for employees, and staff can vote. You have found two options. Choose the option that you prefer. In the next section, you will need to persuade a coworker that your choice is better than the one they prefer.

options.title: Weekly chair yoga in the boardroom
Lunchtime walking club
details: Outdoors – may be cancelled in bad weather
Costs the company $600 a year for prizes

other.title: Monthly massage therapist visits
details: One day a month, 10-minute chair massages
Booked online, first come, first served

t5.persuade: Your coworker prefers the monthly massage therapist visits. Persuade your coworker that your choice is better.
t5.model: I know the massages sound amazing, and who wouldn’t want one? But I really think the walking club is the better choice. First, look at how many people it helps. The massage therapist only has about forty spots a month, and they’ll be gone in five minutes. We have over a hundred and fifty people here. The walking club is open to everybody, three times a week. Second, a ten-minute massage once a month feels nice, but it doesn’t change anyone’s health. Walking thirty minutes three times a week actually builds a habit, and the step challenge keeps people motivated. Third, it’s far cheaper. Six hundred dollars versus forty-five hundred means the company could put the savings toward other things. Yes, we might lose a few walks in bad weather, but we can always walk inside the mall next door.

t6.situation: Your elderly neighbour lives alone and has fallen twice in the past month. The second time, she could not get up for an hour until you heard her calling. She has asked you not to tell her son, who lives in another province, because she is afraid he will move her into a care home.
options: Talk to your neighbour and try to convince her to accept more help.
Call her son and explain what has been happening.
t6.note: Choose ONE option and speak to that person.
t6.model: Margaret, can I sit down with you for a minute? I want to talk about last Tuesday. When I heard you calling and found you on the kitchen floor, I was really scared. You told me you’d been there for an hour. I know you don’t want me to call Tom, and I promised I wouldn’t, but I’m worried that next time I might not hear you. I completely understand that you want to stay in your own home. I want that for you too. So could we look at some options together? There are medical alert buttons you wear on your wrist, and if you fall, you just press it and someone comes right away. We could also ask your doctor about a physiotherapist to help with your balance. I’d even help you call the home-care office. Would you be willing to try?

t7.prompt: Some people believe restaurants should be required to display the results of their most recent health inspection on a sign in their front window. Others think this would unfairly damage businesses over minor problems. What is your opinion? Explain your reasons.
t7.model: In my opinion, restaurants should be required to post their inspection results in the window. My main reason is that customers have a right to know whether the place they’re eating at is safe. When I walk into a restaurant, I can see the dining room, but I have no idea what the kitchen looks like, how food is stored, or whether staff wash their hands. Inspectors already collect that information, and we pay for those inspections with our taxes, so it makes sense to share the results where people can actually see them. A second reason is that it would encourage restaurants to keep their standards high all the time, not just when an inspector is expected. In cities that use a simple colour or letter system, research has shown that kitchens tend to improve, because no owner wants a bad grade in the window. I do understand the concern about minor problems, like a cracked tile, hurting a business. That’s why the system should be fair. Small issues could be noted without lowering the grade, and restaurants should be able to request a quick re-inspection once a problem is fixed. With those protections, I think a public sign would benefit both customers and good restaurants.

scene.alt: A plaza in front of a modern light-blue building labelled “HEALTH CENTRE”. In the middle of the plaza stands a giant grey stone statue of a runner, about three times taller than a real person, shown in mid-stride with arms swinging. At its base, a small real man in a yellow shirt stands looking up and pointing at it, and a woman in a pink dress is taking a photo with a camera. A boy in a red shirt runs past the statue, copying its pose. On the left, there is a tree, a bench and a streetlamp, and a few clouds are in the sky.

t8.prompt: A new statue has just been installed outside your community’s new health centre. Call a friend who has not seen it yet, describe the statue, and explain whether you think it suits the location. Your friend cannot see the picture.
t8.model: Hey Lucas, have you been past the new health centre on Front Street yet? You have to see what they put in the plaza. It’s a giant stone statue of a runner – I’d say it’s about three times taller than a real person. It’s all grey, and it’s caught in the middle of a stride, with one leg forward and its arms swinging, like it’s about to sprint right across the road. When I was there, a guy was pointing up at it, a woman was taking photos, and a little boy kept running circles around it, copying the pose. Honestly, I think it really suits the location. It sends a clear message about staying active, and it’s already getting people’s attention. My only complaint is that it’s a bit grey and serious. A splash of colour would make it more cheerful. Go and check it out!
